explanations.explanation: This neuron flags heading/title tokens – especially those in all‐caps or wrapped in formatting markers (e.g. **bold**, “NOT RECOMMENDED…” banners, court-name headers, date stamps). It marks the boundaries of document sections (titles, metadata lines, section dividers).

This neuron is basically a suffix‐detector: it lights up on subword endings that carry key grammatical or derivational meaning (most prominently the “n’t” of English negation—don’t, couldn’t, isn’t, doesn’t—and on other common suffixes like -ive/-ively, -ographic, -itude, etc.).

This neuron seems to light up whenever the model sees a standalone/topic‐label noun or noun‐like subword used as a heading or category marker—think section titles or classification labels such as “Antiquity,” “conference,” “casinos,” “non-aesthetic,” “aspects,” “century,” etc.

explanations.explanation: This neuron flags the little “glue” pieces that mark boundaries or transitions in text—things like the verbal particles in phrasal verbs (out in “point out,” up in “pick up”), adverbial pivots (however), pivot phrases (account in “taking into account”), plus the punctuation‐oriented tokens that start or end code or markup blocks (brackets, comment markers, XML tags, underscores, dashes). In short, it detects the words and symbols that signal discourse or formatting edges.

This feature detects the presence of open‐source license boilerplate in code comments (e.g. “Copyright (C) …”, “This program is free software…”, “Licensed under the GNU/Apache License,” warranty disclaimers, etc.).
This feature fires on the closing “**” markdown bold delimiter that marks the end of a headline/title and the boundary into the article body.
This feature fires on the “top‐of‐file” or “section” header boilerplate – i.e. copyright/license blocks, comment‐banner separators, include directives and other leading metadata or titles.

explanations.explanation: This is essentially a character-n-gram detector that fires on the two- or three-letter suffixes you see at the ends of capitalized words—especially proper names. In other words, it has learned to spot common name-ending letter sequences (e.g. “gr,” “rie,” “ert,” “elle,” “ar,” “ad,” “cl,” “ib,” etc.).

This neuron is basically a “boilerplate‐header” detector: it fires on C‐style comment markers (`/*`, `*`, `*/`) and the all‐caps copyright/license boilerplate (e.g. “Copyright,” “DO NOT ALTER OR REMOVE COPYRIGHT NOTICES OR THIS FILE HEADER,” “GNU General Public License,” etc.).
This neuron is essentially picking up on “bold” emphasis markers (the double‐asterisks) and the items they surround—i.e. tokens rendered in strong emphasis (case numbers, headings, code tags, etc.)
